topic: HNSW vs IVF indexing for vector search

docs.title: ANN-Benchmarks summary (2024)
docs.text: Across standard approximate-nearest-neighbor benchmarks, IVF (inverted-file) indexes reach higher recall at a given query latency than HNSW graphs, because the coarse-quantizer probe lands directly in the right partition. The tradeoff is memory: IVF keeps per-partition posting lists that make its in-memory footprint substantially larger than an HNSW index over the same data.

docs.title: FAISS wiki: HNSW-PQ
docs.text: HNSW combined with Product Quantization (HNSW-PQ) compresses each stored vector into a short code. This cuts index memory roughly 10-20x versus storing full float32 vectors, at the cost of some recall lost to quantization error.

docs.title: Vector database engineering blog (2024)
docs.text: In production we default to IVF when recall at low latency is the priority: in our own tests IVF reached higher recall than HNSW at the same query latency. The recurring operational cost is memory: IVF uses noticeably more RAM per vector than an HNSW graph, which shows up directly in instance sizing.

docs.title: Scaling ANN postmortem
docs.text: Beyond roughly one billion vectors we found IVF unworkable: its coarse quantizer needs a full retrain as the dataset grows, and rebalancing partitions stalls ingestion. HNSW was the only index that held up at billion scale, so that is what we standardized on.

docs.title: Distributed ANN design doc (2024)
docs.text: HNSW degrades past about one billion vectors: graph degree and memory grow until a single shard can no longer hold the index and traversal thrashes. IVF with sharding across nodes was the only approach that stayed workable at billion scale for us.

docs.title: Top 10 vector index tips
docs.text: Tip 4: for most workloads HNSW gives better recall than IVF at the same latency, so HNSW is the safer default pick when you are unsure.
